161: B is correct because an S3 bucket can trigger a Lambda function directly on new object arrivals, making the processing fully serverless and event-driven. Lambda automatically scales to handle thousands of executions per day without any instances to manage, which maximizes scalability and minimizes operational overhead. Aurora provides a highly available, compatible database target for the results, whereas the other options require managing EC2 instances or containers continuously.
162: A is correct because Amazon FSx for Lustre is a high performance parallel file system designed for Linux HPC workloads with hundreds of Spot instances accessing it concurrently. FSx for Lustre integrates natively with Amazon S3, so on-premises data can be copied to S3 for long-term persistent storage and linked into the Lustre file system for high throughput reads and writes of datasets and output files. The other options either target Windows workloads or lack a true high performance shared file system integrated with persistent storage.
163: A is correct because Amazon ECR provides a fully managed, scalable registry for the container images. Amazon ECS with the Fargate launch type is serverless, so the company runs containers without provisioning or managing any EC2 infrastructure, delivering high availability with minimal operational overhead. Target tracking scaling automatically adjusts capacity to handle the thousands of users, whereas the EC2 launch type and custom AMI approaches require significantly more management.
164: C is correct because Amazon SQS is a fully managed queue that decouples the sender and processor and can retain messages for up to 14 days, covering the 2 day processing window. A dead-letter queue automatically captures messages that fail processing so they are retained for troubleshooting without blocking the processing of remaining messages, which is exactly the stated requirement. This is the most operationally efficient option because SQS requires no infrastructure to run, unlike self-managed Redis, and unlike SNS or Kinesis it natively supports failed message isolation and long retention.
165: D is correct because an origin access identity restricts S3 bucket access so content can only be retrieved through the CloudFront distribution, preventing users from bypassing the inspection layer. Enabling AWS WAF on the CloudFront distribution ensures all website traffic is inspected by WAF at the edge before any content is served from the S3 origin, satisfying the security policy. The other options either cannot actually force traffic through WAF or are not valid ways to bind WAF inspection to all traffic.
166: D is correct because Amazon CloudFront is a global content delivery network that caches the static HTML pages at edge locations close to users around the world. This delivers low latency for millions of views while offloading the read traffic from the S3 origin, making it the most efficient and effective solution. Presigned URLs, cross-Region replication, and geoproximity routing either do not scale to millions of global viewers cost-effectively or do not cache content at the edge.
167: D is correct because Reserved Instances provide a discounted, always-available capacity floor for the predictable baseline, ensuring continuous processing without downtime. On-Demand instances can absorb the unpredictable intermittent spikes reliably, since they are never interrupted. This is the most cost-effective approach that still guarantees no downtime, whereas Spot instances can be reclaimed at any time and Reserved-only capacity for the maximum would be wasteful.
168: D is correct because a service control policy applied at the root organizational unit in AWS Organizations enforces the deny across every account in the organization automatically. SCPs provide a single, central point of maintenance for permissions and scale to any number of accounts without per-account configuration, unlike cross-account roles. ACLs and security groups are not identity or permission governance mechanisms for restricting AWS service access across an organization.
169: C is correct because AWS Shield Advanced is the managed DDoS protection service specifically designed to detect and mitigate large, sophisticated attacks, including at the Application Load Balancer. It adds near real-time visibility, AWS DDoS Response Team access, and cost protection against attack-related scaling charges, directly reducing DDoS risk. Inspector, Macie, and GuardDuty are vulnerability scanning, data classification, and threat detection services and do not prevent DDoS attacks.
170: C is correct because AWS WAF can be associated with an Application Load Balancer and supports geo-match rules that allow or block requests based on the country of origin. By creating a rule to allow only the specific country and block all others, the requirement is met precisely at the edge of the application. Security groups and network ACLs operate on IP addresses and ports and cannot reliably identify or filter traffic by country.
171: B is correct because Amazon API Gateway provides a fully managed REST API that can absorb the large burst of holiday inquiries, and AWS Lambda scales automatically and elastically with each request. This serverless combination handles the seasonal spikes without provisioning capacity ahead of time, and the company pays only for actual usage. The EC2 and ALB based options require capacity planning and management and do not scale as elastically.
172: C is correct because CloudFront field-level encryption encrypts sensitive user input fields, such as personally identifiable information, at the edge before the data travels through the application stack. Only specific trusted applications holding the corresponding private keys can decrypt those fields, restricting access throughout the entire stack on top of HTTPS. Signed URLs and cookies control access to content but do not protect submitted sensitive data.
173: B is correct because an Amazon CloudFront web distribution caches the S3 videos and images at edge locations worldwide, serving millions of users from cache instead of the origin. Since the content is identical for all users, it is highly cacheable, which reduces the load on the S3 origin and origin egress costs. This is the most cost-effective option, as caching services like ElastiCache in front of web servers do not cache S3 objects directly, and Global Accelerator does not cache content.
174: B is correct because spreading the Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones eliminates a single point of failure at the Zone level while the ALB continues to distribute traffic, meeting the high availability requirement without modifying the application. Using multiple Availability Zones within the Region is the standard HA pattern, whereas deploying across Regions would add complexity and cost beyond what is required.
175: B is correct because Amazon RDS Proxy pools and multiplexes database connections between Lambda and Aurora, dramatically reducing the number of open connections that caused the high CPU and memory utilization. Modifying the Lambda function to connect to the proxy endpoint is a minimal change to the application, meeting the requirement of the least possible modifications while preventing timeout errors during order surges. The other options require significant re-architecture or do not address the connection exhaustion root cause.
176: A is correct because a VPC endpoint for DynamoDB is a gateway endpoint that lets EC2 instances in private subnets reach the table through the AWS private network without traversing the internet. This is the most secure option since no NAT, internet gateway, or public IP is needed, and traffic never leaves the AWS network. NAT gateways, NAT instances, and internet gateets all route traffic outside the private AWS network path.
177: B is correct because Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed, purpose-built caching layer for DynamoDB that delivers microsecond response times for read-intensive workloads. The application only needs to point to the DAX endpoint instead of the table endpoint, so performance improves without reconfiguring the application or adding operational burden. ElastiCache options require application changes and cache management, and global tables address multi-Region replication rather than read latency.
178: A is correct because AWS Backup provides a single, centralized, fully managed service to back up EC2 instances and RDS databases and copy those backups to a separate Region. This achieves cross-Region backup protection with the least operational overhead because backup plans, schedules, and retention are managed in one place. The DLM, AMI plus read replica, and snapshot export plus S3 CRR options require considerably more manual orchestration and ongoing administration.
179: A is correct because an IAM role that grants read access to the SecureString parameter and decrypt permission on the KMS key that encrypts it can be assigned to the EC2 instance as an instance profile. The application on the instance then securely retrieves the database credentials without hardcoding secrets, and only that role can decrypt the parameter. IAM policies cannot be assigned directly to an EC2 instance, and trust relationships between resources as described in the other options are not valid mechanisms for this access.
180: B is correct because AWS Shield Advanced provides detection and mitigation of large, sophisticated DDoS attacks and can be attached directly to the Network Load Balancer, adding the DDoS Response Team and attack visibility needed for a large-scale event. C is correct because AWS WAF can be associated with Amazon API Gateway, where it inspects API traffic and blocks web exploits such as SQL injection before requests reach the EC2 backend. Together, WAF on the API entry point and Shield Advanced on the NLB provide layered protection against both application-layer exploits and volumetric DDoS attacks, whereas Shield Standard alone does not mitigate sophisticated attacks and GuardDuty only detects rather than prevents them.
